title: CLO International Academic Month Issue 3 (Part 2) The Application of CLO3D at the University of Applied Sciences in Sigmaringen
description: In this month's academic video, Professor Christian Kaiser from Sigmaringen University of Applied Sciences shares the practical application of CLO3D in daily clothing education. As a professor of engineering, his interdisciplinary teaching experience demonstrates the potential for the practical use of CLO3D software in other fields. After the course, students used the software for challenges, designing many impressive works! Click the video to watch!

summary: ```markdown # CLO International Academic Month Issue 3 (Part 2) ## The Application of CLO3D at the University of Applied Sciences in Sigmaringen ### Introduction Okay, Professor Kaeser, we can start now whenever you are ready. Okay, thank you. So I'm going to share my screen. Perfect. You can see it. Yeah, I can see it. Okay, awesome. Thank you very much. I would like to welcome all of you also from my side. Um, I guess I have already been introduced. My name is Christian Kaiser. I am a professor at the University of Albstadt-Sigmaringen in the textile department. We are educating textile and garment engineers. ### Background My scientific background is that I am an engineering cybernetician, which means actually that I'm a control engineer or systems engineer. I got in touch with the textile topics during my studies at the University of Stuttgart. What I would like to give you a short overview and some insights into is how our university introduced CLO3D in our curriculum. Before I joined Albstadt-Sigmaringen University in 2018, 3D was not a focus point in our teaching classes. My personal background is that I have been a 3D user since 2010, so I would say I am one of the first users in Europe. ### Importance of 3D in Textile Education As I am not from the garment and textile industry, it was not hard to convince myself that 3D development and 3D simulation is state of the art in mechanical engineering, aerospace, and all other mechanical engineering disciplines. It’s pretty obvious that 3D development and 3D visualization of garments should also be implemented in the future. I hope we can achieve that in the textile industry as soon as possible. ### Implementation of 3D Classes Starting with what we did to implement 3D classes based on CLO at our bachelor's degree, the starting point was the winter semester in 2019 to 2020. There, we started introducing 3D models and using CLO3D within our bachelor courses. At that time, it started with one course. Pretty soon, a colleague of mine, who is a designer, and I entered the academic workshop of CLO in Munich, Germany. This was our start, where we refined our pre-existing understanding of 3D simulation with this type of software. Both of us were skilled in terms of other software, as we use multiple 3D software at our university. However, this workshop was a game changer because it allowed us to speed up our tutorial database and online courses, as well as enhance the quality of our presence teaching. ### Student Projects and Curriculum Optimization Pretty soon after this, we also had our first students' 3D project in 2020, followed by our second one just the next semester. After this curriculum, we started optimizing our tutorial database. As a control engineer, I personally live in a feedback loop. Every kind of teaching and every type of action I’m responsible for starts with some kind of steering impulse, such as starting with the curriculum. We optimize each of our lectures regularly based on student feedback and market developments, whether software-wise or application-wise. By mid-2021, we had our first big run-through, which we used to optimize our tutorial database and also attended a second academic workshop at CLO in Munich. In fact, the second workshop was not that necessary anymore because we were already skilled in what we were doing. However, it was super helpful for two reasons: networking and learning from super active and skilled players. ### Challenges in Curriculum Integration What were the challenges we faced? The main challenge was embedding 3D in current curricula. You may have experienced this issue: having current lessons while needing to focus on important areas such as sewing, textiles, CAD, and the new entry of 3D, which means you really have to focus. For us, the general focus points were, first of all, mechanics, digital sewing, and then going to two application areas: virtual fit and the 3D design part. ### Student Project Example What you see on the right side is the work of my students in 2021, where they, based on the materials I was teaching them, had to experience their own small projects, such as developing a pattern in 2D, transferring the data. In this case, we used Electra's 2D system to CLO to arrange patterns, do the first swings, debug, and optimize the draping of the garment. ### Embedding 3D Skills I already mentioned embedding 3D. I use this word by purpose because embedding is different from an add-on. In European teaching, many universities understand 3D skills as add-ons to traditional textile and garment skills. In my opinion, this point of view is mistaken. It’s not an add-on; it’s a basic skill. Just as students must learn to sew and develop patterns by hand, they must also build 3D competencies. This means our students do not have any choice regarding 3D classes for a significant time. The skills we want to transfer to our students include digital construction lessons that split between hand-based pattern construction, CAD, and the 3D simulation of these CAD patterns. ### Close Feedback Loop This process allows the students to have a close feedback loop. What they develop by hand, they can see how to implement on the computer, and they can observe the drape in 3D on a defined human model. We do this at a standard level in Digital Construction 2 and go into more advanced 2D and 3D skills in Digital Construction 3. In Digital Construction 4, we shift our focus to high-end simulation and rendering because having digital twins of garments on the technical side is one thing, but enabling high-end visual communication is another crucial part. ### Standard Skill Development Having this so far enables students to use 3D as a standard skill in various projects. These projects may include project lectures or projects in different lectures. For example, we have lectures focusing on uncommon sewing and tufting solutions like welding and gluing, where students are developing rain jackets. Since we started implementing this type of curriculum, students use 3D for prototyping the garments they develop in these lectures. This means 3D is a real standard skill. While the professor for these lectures may not be a 3D expert, the students choose to utilize 3D on their own, which is something I’m really proud of. ### Continuous Improvement For sure, I must admit that for the advanced lectures, we really pushed the students and raised awareness. But now, students are adopting and using these skills independently. I would say 3D is a standard skill for our students by the third semester, usable in further design lectures, 3D print design, 3D knit design, alternative sewing technologies, and more. ### Success Factors Another success factor was the CLO academic workshop. For me personally, it was less about teaching the mechanics of the 3D software but more about the excellent tutorial database provided by CLO in these workshops. This really helped me build up tutorials and curricula for my students in a super lean and handy way. I highly recommend making use of opportunities like this; they are incredibly helpful. Another success factor in our case is our team. You may have already heard that I’m more of the techie. Design and aesthetics are not my core competencies; I focus on whether the technical work is done correctly. My colleague, Maria Baum, is the creative part—a design professor who helps students use the tools I teach them in a super creative way, enabling them to realize complex and innovative designs. Together, we create the best learning experience depending on the type of application. ### Online Teaching Platform I built an online teaching platform for all the software we use in our textile classes, featuring video tutorials. I strongly believe that it is not a question of whether you do 3D; it’s about how well you do it. In my opinion, 3D is one of the most important tools for the industry for the next five to ten years. ### Continuous Optimization Moreover, during the pandemic, it became even more critical to enable students to choose their own teaching experience. We constantly optimize our tutorial database, scripts, and teaching materials for in-person lessons. ### Example of 3D Design Impact Here you see a simple example from a 3D design class. You may face trust issues in the industry regarding whether 3D has any positive impact on work. In this case, you see a regular T-shirt—a "white shell"—draped with different textures like mesh, knit, jersey, and shiny materials. The appearance of the T-shirt completely depends on the type of material used. If you are a T-shirt or trousers manufacturer, building white shell libraries can significantly speed up your processes. This approach lightens your workflow because, traditionally, industry relies on swatches or prototypes, which includes latency until prototypes are manufactured. ### Simulation Ingredients I also teach students about the ingredients of a good simulation. We focus on the fabric, pattern, and human model in 3D. When it comes to the fabric, we discuss different types of maps and their uses. It’s crucial to improve map quality—sharp maps that are not blurry and suitable for high-end rendering. Alternatively, students can use their smartphones to take short snippets for assessment purposes. Here you see work from my students, all from 2021. They are now even more skilled than at that time. We also use various tools alongside
